newsitem.title: ITALY: FORECAST - Italy growth seen sluggish until end-1997.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Italy growth seen sluggish until end-1997.

text.p: Italy's languishing economy is unlikely to emerge from the doldrums until the fourth quarter of 1997 when gross domestic product (GDP) growth will inch up from one percent and continue rising in 1998, analysts said.
A Reuter quarterly poll of 16 analysts showed a mean forecast for 1997 GDP growth of 1.1 percent against an estimate three months ago of 1.2 percent. The poll was conducted from April 1 to 3.

The latest government growth target for this year is 1.2 percent, revised downwards from a previous 2.0 percent and compared with actual 1996 GDP growth of 0.7 percent. The Bank of Italy sees growth this year of little more than one percent.
Analysts said that after a disappointing first quarter Italian economic growth will improve, thanks to the favourable effect of an upturn in other European economies.

"Italian growth reached a nadir in the first quarter. But in the second quarter we expect to see the first signs of a reversing trend thanks to the pick-up in the rest of Europe and the strong dollar which favours Italian exports to non-EU countries," said Ilaria Fornari, economist at JP Morgan.

Paolo Casadio, economist at Credito Italiano, said data seasonally-adjusted for different totals of working days "showed that the economy picked up, even though very slightly, in the fourth quarter of 1996."

However, he said the recovery in the rest of Europe would only have a limited impact as Italy had lost some foreign market share because Italian companies' price policies had not fully offset the lira's appreciation.

Analysts said that while foreign demand would be the most positive factor in Italy's recovery, on the domestic front they did not see a sharp pick-up in consumption nor did they expect for the moment investments and inventories to give a significant contribution to growth.
"Durable goods consumption remains low. This worries producers causing a negative impact on investments and inventories," Paolo Pizzoli, analyst at Banca Akros, said.
"Both fiscal and monetary policy are restrictive in Italy. Consumption is limited by fears of new taxes," Fornari added.

But in the fairly glum domestic scenario there are slight positive signs coming from an increase in disposable income with wages rising more than inflation and a revival of Italy's depressed auto market due to the government's new car buying incentive programme.

Analysts see investment rising by less than two percent in 1997. "Italian companies are still growing less than the economy as a whole. Industry first wants to see a pick-up in demand before restarting investing and accumulating stocks," Casadio said.

The mean forecast for 1997 industrial production was for limited growth of 0.8 percent, rising progressively from a fall of 1.7 percent in the first three months of the year to a 2.6 percent increase in the fourth quarter.

Unemployment is seen little changed with a mean forecast of 12.3 percent which could decline to 12.0 percent in 1998 if planned government policy measures to create jobs bore fruit. In the quarter to January, the jobless rate stood at 12.4 percent.
